mainTopic: Which injuries free an עבד כנעני, whether he needs a גט שחרור, and the details of indirect, partial and accidental injuries
overview: This amud keeps working out which injuries free an עבד כנעני. The גמרא explains why the תורה names both a tooth and an eye. It then reads the פסוק as a כלל ופרט וכלל with a ריבוי, so any visible injury that does not heal frees the slave, even if the limb still works. A ברייתא then brings a מחלוקת about whether the freed slave also needs a גט שחרור. רבי שמעון learns from a divorced wife that a document is needed, and רבי מאיר reads ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ to mean he is free at once. Next come cases: a blow near the eye or ear, which leads רב אשי to explain that a person hurt by noise really frightened himself. Then the גמרא discusses a weakened eye or loosened tooth, and a doctor master who blinds his slave while treating him, where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires intent to destroy. רב ששת rules that removing an already-blind eye frees the slave, with support from the law of bird קרבנות. A new ruling from רב begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the תורה needed both tooth and eye
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its צריכותא. With only ״שן״, we might include a baby tooth. With only ״עין״, we might include only body parts a person is born with and leave out teeth.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the תורה wrote only 'tooth,' we would think even a baby tooth frees the slave, so it wrote 'eye.' If it wrote only 'eye,' we would think only body parts a person is born with count, and a tooth would not. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to the question of why the פסוק mentions both a tooth and an eye. Each word stops us from making a different mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With only ״שן״, we might include a baby tooth, which grows back. ״עין״ teaches that the injury must be to a part that does not grow back. With only ״עין״, we might think it must be a part a person is born with, and teeth come in later, so ״שן״ teaches that teeth count too.

keyTerms.meaning: A baby tooth (literally a 'milk tooth'), which falls out and grows back
'The Merciful One', a name for ה׳ as the author of the תורה
'I would have thought', a mistaken first idea
Created with him, meaning a body part a person already has at birth
'It is necessary', the closing word of a צריכותא showing that both words of the פסוק are needed

steps.whatToRemember: ״שן״ and ״עין״ each teach something. ״עין״ shows the injured part must not grow back, and ״שן״ shows it does not have to be a part he was born with.

phrases.english: even a baby tooth [would free him],
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from just before: if the תורה wrote only 'tooth,' you might think even a baby tooth counts.

phrases.english: so the Merciful One wrote 'eye.'
And if the Merciful One had written only 'eye,'

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא מָה עַיִן שֶׁנִּבְרָא עִמּוֹ
phrases.english: I would have said: just as an eye was created with him,
so too anything that was created with him [counts],
but a tooth would not.
phrases.notes: Teeth come in after birth, so you might think they are left out.

phrases.english: So it is necessary [to write both].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a צריכותא that began just before this section
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each word blocks a different wrong conclusion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With one word only, we would either include a baby tooth or leave out all teeth
steps.terutzMaskana: Both words are needed: the part must not grow back, but it does not have to be there from birth

steps.title: Challenge: maybe only a tooth and an eye count
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests reading the פסוק as a כלל ופרט. That would mean only a tooth and an eye free the slave, and no other limb.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say this: 'If a man strikes' is a general statement, and 'tooth and eye' is the detail. With a general statement followed by a detail, only what is in the detail is included. So a tooth and an eye count, and nothing else does!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that other limbs also free a slave. It uses the rule of כלל ופרט to suggest that only a tooth and an eye count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One of the rules for reading the תורה says that when a general phrase is followed by a specific detail, the general phrase is limited to that detail. ״כי יכה״ is general and ״שן ועין״ is the detail, so other limbs would be left out.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But say...', introducing a different way to read the פסוק
A general statement in a פסוק
A specific detail in a פסוק
A rule: a general statement followed by a detail includes only the detail

steps.confusionAlert: Earlier the גמרא assumed other limbs also free a slave. Here it is testing that assumption, not deciding against it.

phrases.english: But say: 'If a man strikes' is a general statement,
phrases.notes: שמות 21:26

phrases.english: 'tooth and eye' is a detail.
With a general statement followed by a detail,
the general statement includes only what is in the detail.
A tooth and an eye count,
and nothing else does!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the assumption that limbs other than tooth and eye are included
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that other limbs also free a slave
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read as a כלל ופרט, the פסוק limits freedom to the tooth and eye named in the detail

steps.title: Answer: the פסוק generalizes again at the end
steps.stepSummary: ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ is a second general statement, so the פסוק is a כלל ופרט וכלל. This includes everything similar to tooth and eye: visible blemishes that do not grow back.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He shall send him free' is the פסוק going back and generalizing. With general, detail, and general, you include only things like the detail. The detail is a visible blemish that does not grow back, so all visible blemishes that do not grow back are included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק ends with another general phrase. That changes the rule we use and widens what is included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a כלל ופרט וכלל, we include anything that shares the main features of the detail. A tooth and an eye are both visible and do not grow back, so any injury with those two features frees the slave.

keyTerms.meaning: 'He shall send him free', the closing words of the פסוק
It went back and generalized, meaning a second general statement
General, detail, general: we include things similar to the detail
A visible blemish, one that can be seen

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the basic rule: an injury frees an עבד כנעני if it is a visible blemish that does not grow back.

phrases.english: 'He shall send him free': the פסוק went back and generalized.
With general, detail, and general,

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט,
phrases.english: you may include only what is similar to the detail.
Just as the detail that is spelled out
is a visible blemish, and they do not grow back,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי וְאֵינָן חוֹזְרִין.
phrases.english: so too all visible blemishes that do not grow back [count].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the כלל ופרט challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the פסוק's structure as a כלל ופרט וכלל
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only a tooth and an eye count
steps.terutzMaskana: Any visible blemish that does not grow back counts

steps.title: Why not require that the limb stop working too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a third feature shared by tooth and eye: the limb stops working. But a ברייתא says a slave goes free when his beard is pulled out and a bone is loosened, even though nothing stops working.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, we could say: the detail is a visible blemish where the limb stops working and does not grow back, so only injuries with all those features should count. Then why does a ברייתא teach that if the master pulled out his beard and loosened a bone, the slave goes free?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes the comparison further by adding a third feature, that the limb stops working. It then challenges this from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tooth and an eye also share the fact that losing them stops a function, like chewing or seeing. If we copied every feature, a beard and jawbone injury would not count, since nothing stops working. Yet the ברייתא says the slave goes free.

keyTerms.meaning: The limb stops doing its job
'Why, then, was it taught...?', introducing a ברייתא that contradicts the idea

phrases.english: If so: just as the detail that is spelled out
is visible blemishes where the limb stops working
and it does not grow back,
so too all visible blemishes
that do not grow back and where the limb stops working [should count].
Why, then, was it taught in a ברייתא:
if he pulled out his beard and loosened a bone there,
the slave goes free through them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes the comparison from the previous answer further, then challenges it from a ברייתא
steps.kashyaTarget: How far the comparison to tooth and eye should go
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If every feature of the detail is required, the beard and jawbone case should not free the slave, yet the ברייתא says it does

steps.title: Answer: ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ widens the law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ is a ריבוי, a widening phrase. So the injury does not need to stop the limb from working.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He shall send him free' is a widening phrase.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from the ברייתא. The closing words of the פסוק widen the law so that the limb does not have to stop working.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of treating ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ only as a second כלל, the גמרא reads it as a ריבוי, which includes more. Only two features are required: visible, and does not grow back. The third feature, that the limb stops working, is dropped, so the beard and jawbone case is included.

keyTerms.meaning: A ריבוי: a phrase that widens the law to include more cases

steps.whatToRemember: A slave goes free from any visible injury that does not grow back, even if the limb still works. This comes from the widening phrase ״לחפשי ישלחנו״.

phrases.english: 'He shall send him free'
is a widening phrase.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge from the beard and jawbone ברייתא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the closing phrase as a ריבוי that widens the law
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The injury must also stop the limb from working
steps.terutzMaskana: Visible and not growing back is enough; the limb does not have to stop working

steps.title: If it is a widening phrase, why doesn't a temporary injury free the slave?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ריבוי. If ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ widens the law, it should include even a hand that withered but will heal. Yet a ברייתא says that does not free the slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if it is a widening phrase, then even if the master hit the slave's hand and it withered but will heal, the slave should go free. So why does a ברייתא teach that in that case the slave does not go free?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from Step 5. If the phrase is a ריבוי, why is a temporary injury left out?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 said ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ is a ריבוי, so the injury does not need to stop the limb from working. If the phrase widens that much, it seems it should also include an injury that heals. But a ברייתא rules that a hand that withered and will recover does not free the slave.

keyTerms.meaning: A widening phrase that adds more cases to a law
It withered or shriveled (here, the hand stopped working for a while)
Why then was it taught in a ברייתא?

phrases.english: But if it is a widening phrase,
phrases.notes: This refers back to ״לחפשי ישלחנו״, which the גמרא just called a widening phrase.

phrases.english: then even if he struck him on his hand and it withered
and it will eventually recover, also [the slave should go free],
so why was it taught:

phrases.aramaic: הִכָּהוּ עַל יָדוֹ וְצָמְתָה וְסוֹפָהּ לַחְזוֹר –
phrases.english: If he struck him on his hand and it withered but will eventually recover,
the slave does not go free because of it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how far the ריבוי from Step 5 reaches
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ is a ריבוי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ריבוי should include temporary injuries too, but a ברייתא excludes them

steps.title: Tooth and eye must still limit the law
steps.stepSummary: If temporary injuries were included, the examples of שן and עין would teach nothing. So the ריבוי only adds injuries that are permanent, like a tooth or eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what would the תורה gain by mentioning tooth and eye?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ריבוי cannot be unlimited. The examples of tooth and eye must still mean something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The widening phrase removes only the need for the limb to stop working. The details of tooth and eye still set limits: the blemish must be visible and permanent. A hand that will heal is not like a tooth or eye, so it does not free the slave.

keyTerms.meaning: What did it accomplish? What purpose does it serve?

steps.whatToRemember: ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ widens the law past the need for the limb to stop working, but the injury must still be permanent like a tooth or eye.

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: Meaning: if even injuries that heal were included.

phrases.english: what purpose do tooth and eye serve?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, שֵׁן וָעַיִן מַאי אַהֲנִי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the ריבוי by the details of the פרט
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ריבוי includes every injury, even one that heals
steps.terutzMaskana: The ריבוי drops only the need for the limb to stop working; the injury must still be permanent like שן and עין

steps.title: Does the freed slave need a release document?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא brings a מחלוקת. רבי שמעון, רבי אליעזר and רבי עקיבא say the slave needs a גט שחרור. רבי מאיר and רבי טרפון say he does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: for all of these injuries the slave goes free, and he needs a release document. This is רבי שמעון's view. רבי מאיר says he does not need one. רבי אליעזר says he needs one. רבי טרפון says he does not need one. רבי עקיבא says he needs one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ברייתא. Once the slave has a right to go free, does the master still have to write him a release document?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees the slave goes free. The only question is how the freedom takes effect. Either it happens by itself the moment he is injured, or the master must formally release him with a גט שחרור.

keyTerms.meaning: In all of them (all the limbs that free a slave)
A document that frees a slave

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody here says the slave stays a slave. The מחלוקת is only whether he also needs a גט שחרור.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: with regard to all of them,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means all the limbs the גמרא listed earlier on this daf that free a slave.

phrases.english: a slave goes free through them,
and he needs a release document,
these are the words of Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Meir says: he does not need one.
Rabbi Eliezer says: he needs one.
Rabbi Tarfon says: he does not need one.
Rabbi Akiva says: he needs one.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בְּכוּלָּם, עֶבֶד יוֹצֵא בָּהֶם לְחֵירוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from which injuries free a slave to how the freedom takes effect
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Tannaim disagree whether a slave freed by an injury needs a גט שחרור

steps.title: The deciders split the ruling
steps.stepSummary: The מכריעים rule like רבי טרפון for tooth and eye, because the תורה gave the slave that right directly. They rule like רבי עקיבא for other limbs, calling that a קנס חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Those who decide before the חכמים say: רבי טרפון seems right about tooth and eye, since the תורה granted him freedom. רבי עקיבא seems right about the other limbs, since it is a penalty of the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: A group of deciders offers a middle path between the two sides. Their reason for the other limbs will be challenged in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Tooth and eye are written in the תורה, so freedom comes by itself and no document is needed. For other limbs they say a document is needed, and they explain this by calling it a rabbinic penalty. That explanation is about to be questioned.

keyTerms.meaning: Granted it to him (the Torah gave him this right)
A penalty made by the Sages

phrases.english: Those who decide before the Sages say:

phrases.aramaic: נִרְאִין דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן בְּשֵׁן וָעַיִן,
phrases.english: The words of Rabbi Tarfon seem right regarding tooth and eye,
since the Torah granted it to him,
and the words of Rabbi Akiva regarding the other limbs,
since it is a penalty of the Sages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a compromise ruling on the מחלוקת of Step 8
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No גט for tooth and eye; a גט is needed for other limbs

steps.title: It's not a penalty, it comes from the פסוקים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects. The other limbs were learned from the פסוקים through the כלל ופרט וכלל, so how can they be called a rabbinic penalty?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it a penalty? We learn it from the פסוקים!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason the deciders gave for the other limbs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא learned the other limbs from the פסוק by a כלל ופרט וכלל. That makes them Torah law, not a penalty the Sages added. So calling it a קנס does not fit.

keyTerms.meaning: We are learning it from the פסוקים

phrases.english: Is it a penalty?!
We are expounding the verses!
phrases.notes: This points back to the כלל ופרט וכלל from Steps 2 and 3.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in Step 9
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The other limbs come from a Torah derivation, so they cannot be a rabbinic penalty

steps.title: It means a Sages' derivation
steps.stepSummary: The deciders really meant מדרש חכמים. The other limbs are Torah law, but they are learned through the Sages' derivation rather than written outright, so a document is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: since it is learned by the Sages' derivation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא corrects the wording of the deciders' reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is not Torah law versus rabbinic law. It is written outright versus learned through a derivation. Because the other limbs are not written plainly in the פסוק, the slave's freedom there needs a גט שחרור.

keyTerms.meaning: A law the Sages learn from the פסוק through a derivation

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the other limbs became rabbinic. They are still Torah law, just learned through a derivation instead of written outright.

phrases.english: Rather: since it is a derivation of the Sages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 10 by rewording the deciders' reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The other limbs are a rabbinic penalty
steps.terutzMaskana: The other limbs are Torah law learned by derivation, so a גט is needed

steps.title: What is רבי שמעון's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי שמעון requires a גט שחרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבי שמעון's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up an explanation of רבי שמעון's view from the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now we only had the deciders' middle path. Now the גמרא goes back to the original opinions and looks for the source behind requiring a document.

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא of Step 8 to explain רבי שמעון
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for requiring a גט שחרור

steps.title: Learning the slave from a divorced wife
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון learns a גזירה שוה from the word ״שילוח״ (sending away), which appears both for the slave and for a divorced wife. A wife needs a document, so a slave does too.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns ״sending away″ for the slave from ״sending away″ for a wife. Just as a wife is released with a document, so a slave is released with a document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי שמעון compares the slave to a divorced wife through a shared word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave's פסוק says ״ישלחנו״ and the divorce פסוק says ״ושלחה״. Because the same word is used, the rule of one carries over to the other. A wife needs a גט, so a slave needs a גט שחרור.

phrases.english: He learns "sending away" from "sending away" of a woman.
phrases.notes: שמות 21:26 and דברים 24:1.

phrases.english: Just as a woman is released by a document,
so too a slave is also released by a document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of שילוח from a divorced wife: both need a document

steps.title: רבי מאיר: the word order shows he is already free
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר answers that the פסוק puts ״לחפשי″ (to freedom) before ״ישלחנו״ (he shall send him). This shows the slave is already free before any sending, so no document is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי מאיר says: if ״free″ were written at the end, it would be as you say. Now that it says ״to freedom shall he send him″, he is free from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי מאיר responds to רבי שמעון's comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Had the פסוק said ״he shall send him to freedom″, freedom would come only after a sending, like a divorce. Because ״לחפשי״ comes first, the slave is free the moment he is injured. The sending is just letting a free man go, with no document needed.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון compares the slave to a divorced wife, so a document is needed. רבי מאיר reads ״לחפשי״ first, so the slave is free at once and needs no document.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir [would say]:
If "free" had been written at the end,
it would be as you say.
Now that it is written "to freedom shall he send him,"
he is free from the beginning.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי מאיר's reply to רבי שמעון's גזירה שוה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word order ״לחפשי ישלחנו״ shows the slave is free immediately, so no document is needed

steps.title: Striking the eye or ear itself versus striking near it
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that the עבד goes free if the master strikes his eye or ear and blinds or deafens him. If the master strikes near the eye or ear, the עבד does not go free.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: if the master hit him on the eye and blinded it, or on the ear and deafened it, the slave goes free. If he hit near the eye and the slave can't see, or near the ear and he can't hear, the slave does not go free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about which blows to the eye or ear set an עבד free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The organ itself must be struck. If the master hits nearby and the damage comes indirectly, for example from the shock or the noise, the עבד stays a slave. This sets up the next question about whether noise counts as real damage.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If he struck him on his eye and blinded it,
or on his ear and deafened it,
the slave goes out to freedom through them.
If he struck near his eye and he does not see,
or near his ear and he does not hear,
the slave does not go out to freedom through them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הִכָּהוּ עַל עֵינוֹ וְסִמְּאָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic: the details of which injuries free an עבד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a direct blow to the eye or ear frees the עבד. Damage from a blow near the organ does not.

steps.title: Isn't damage caused by sound real damage?
steps.stepSummary: רב שמן asks רב אשי whether the ברייתא means that sound counts for nothing. He points to two rulings where an owner pays for damage done by noise: a rooster that crowed into a glass vessel, and a horse or donkey whose noise broke vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמן said to רב אשי: does this mean sound is nothing? Didn't רמי בר יחזקאל teach that if a rooster stuck its head into a glass vessel, crowed and broke it, the owner pays full damage? And רב יוסף said that the school of רב says: if a horse neighed or a donkey brayed and broke vessels in the house, the owner pays half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שמן challenges the ברייתא. In the laws of damages, noise is treated as something that can really cause damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא suggests that a blow near the ear, which damages only through noise or shock, is not a real injury. Yet in the laws of damages, an owner pays when his animal's noise breaks something. The amounts differ (full or half), but either way sound creates liability, so why shouldn't it count for the עבד?

keyTerms.meaning: It is nothing (has no legal weight)

phrases.english: Rav Shemen said to Rav Ashi:
Is this to say that a sound is nothing?
But didn't Rami bar Yeḥezkel teach:
A rooster that stuck its head
into the airspace of a glass vessel,
and crowed into it and broke it,
the owner pays the full damage.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף, אָמְרִי בֵּי רַב:
phrases.english: And Rav Yosef said that the school of Rav say:
A horse that neighed or a donkey that brayed,
and they broke vessels inside the house,
the owners pay half the damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the second half of the ברייתא in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a blow near the eye or ear does not free the עבד
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the laws of damages, sound can cause real damage that must be paid for. So hearing loss caused by sound should also count.

steps.title: A person is different: he frightens himself
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that a person is different from a glass vessel. Because a person has understanding, the damage comes from his own fear, not straight from the sound.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: a person is different. Since he has understanding, he is the one who frightens himself.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the challenge by separating damage to objects from damage to people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sound physically breaks a glass vessel, so the owner pays. When a person loses his hearing from a noise, the damage really comes from his own fright, so the master did not directly injure him.

phrases.english: He said to him: A person is different,
phrases.notes: "He" is רב אשי, answering רב שמן.

phrases.english: since he has understanding,
it is he who frightens himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב שמן's challenge from step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sound causes damage the same way to objects and to people.
steps.terutzMaskana: Sound physically breaks objects, but a person is hurt by his own fear, so it is not a direct injury by the master.
steps.whatToRemember: Noise can break a vessel directly. When a person is hurt by noise, the cause is his own fright, so it does not count as the master striking him.

steps.title: Support from the law of one who frightens another
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא backs up רב אשי. One who frightens another person is exempt in human court but liable in the laws of Heaven. Shouting into someone's ear and deafening him is exempt, but if he grabbed him first and then shouted, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: one who frightens his friend is exempt by human law but liable by the laws of Heaven. How so? If he shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is exempt. If he grabbed him and shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that damage from fright is not treated as a direct injury.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Deafening someone by shouting is only a Heavenly sin, not a case for a human court, because the injury comes from his fear. Once the shouter physically grabs him, he is liable even in court. This fits רב אשי's answer.

phrases.english: As it was taught:
One who frightens his friend
is exempt by human law
but liable by the laws of Heaven.
How so?
If he shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is exempt;
if he grabbed him and shouted into his ear and deafened him, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to support רב אשי's answer in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: רב אשי's claim that a person hurt by noise has frightened himself
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: one who frightens another is exempt in human court unless he physically took hold of him.

steps.title: A weakened eye or a loosened tooth
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that if the master's blow only weakened the eye or loosened the tooth, the עבד goes free only if he can no longer use it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: if he hit him on the eye and weakened it, or on the tooth and loosened it, and the slave can still use them now, he does not go free. If not, he goes free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about blows that harm the eye or tooth without fully destroying it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether the eye or tooth still works now, after the blow. If it is still usable, the עבד has not lost a limb, so he stays a slave.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
If he struck him on his eye and it weakened,
or on his tooth and it became loose,
if he can use them now,
the slave does not go out to freedom through them;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו – עֶבֶד יוֹצֵא בָּהֶן לְחֵירוּת.
phrases.english: and if not, the slave goes out to freedom through them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הִכָּהוּ עַל עֵינוֹ וְכָהֲתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new set of cases about partly damaged limbs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A weakened eye or loosened tooth frees the עבד only if it can no longer be used.

steps.title: An eye already weak or a tooth already loose before the blow
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא covers an eye that was already weak and was then blinded, or a tooth that was already loose and was then knocked out. The עבד goes free only if he could still use it before the blow.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא taught: if his eye was already weak and the master blinded it, or his tooth was already loose and he knocked it out, then if he could use them before, the slave goes free. If not, he does not go free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that looks at the condition of the eye or tooth before the master struck.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the test looks back in time. If the weak eye or loose tooth still worked before the blow, the master destroyed a working limb, so the עבד goes free. If it was already useless, nothing of value was lost.
steps.whatToRemember: Both ברייתות ask one question: was a working eye or tooth lost? In step 19 we look at whether it works after the blow; here we look at whether it worked before.
steps.confusionAlert: The two ברייתות look like opposites because 'can use it' leads to 'not free' in one and 'free' in the other. In the first, 'now' means after the blow. In the second, 'already' means before the blow.

phrases.english: It was taught in another ברייתא:
Where his eye was weak and the master blinded it,
or his tooth was loose and he knocked it out,
if he was able to use them before,
the slave goes out to freedom through them;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו – אֵין עֶבֶד יוֹצֵא בָּהֶן לְחֵירוּת.
phrases.english: and if not, the slave does not go out to freedom through them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא אִידַּךְ: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיְתָה עֵינוֹ כְּהוּיָה וְסִמְּאָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the opposite case to step 19: the limb was weak before the blow, and the blow destroyed it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the weak eye or loose tooth was usable before the blow, destroying it frees the עבד. If it was not usable, he stays a slave.

steps.title: Why both teachings about a weak eye are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that both ברייתות from steps 19 and 20 are necessary. Each one teaches a case we could not have learned from the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both teachings are needed. If we only had the first one (a healthy eye weakened by the blow until it can't be used), we might think he goes free only because his sight went from strong to weak. But in the second case, where his sight was already weak, we might say he does not go free. And if we only had the second one (a weak eye fully blinded), we might think he goes free only because the eye was blinded completely. But in the first case, where it was not fully blinded, we might say he does not go free. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is showing that the two ברייתות are not repeating each other. Each one covers a case the other would leave in doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Case one: a healthy eye made weak. We might think the עבד goes free only because he lost strong sight. Case two: a weak eye blinded fully. We might think he goes free only because the blindness was total. Since each case has a different reason it might seem special, we need both rulings to show the עבד goes free in each.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary (both teachings are needed)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'the first one' means the ברייתא in step 19 (a healthy eye that was weakened), and 'this one' means the ברייתא in step 20 (a weak eye that was fully blinded). Don't mix them up.

phrases.english: And it is necessary, for if it had taught us only that first one,
phrases.notes: 'That first one' is the ברייתא about a healthy eye that the master's blow made weak.

phrases.english: [we would say he goes free] because at first his eyesight was strong
and now his eyesight is weak.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּמֵעִיקָּרָא נָמֵי נְהוֹרָא כְּחִישָׁא –
phrases.english: But here, where at first his eyesight was also weak,
I would say: no, he does not go free.
And if it had taught us only this one,
[we would say he goes free] because he blinded him completely,
but there, where he did not blind him completely,
I would say: no. So both are necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the two ברייתות in steps 19 and 20 are both needed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both rulings are needed. A healthy eye weakened so much that it can no longer be used frees the עבד, and a weak eye that is fully blinded also frees him, as long as it was usable before.

steps.title: The doctor master who blinds his slave while treating him
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a master who is a doctor blinds his עבד's eye or knocks out his tooth while treating him, the עבד goes free.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: If the master was a doctor, and the slave asked him to put medicine on his eye and he blinded it, or to drill his tooth and he knocked it out, the slave has the last laugh on his master and goes free.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a master who hurt his עבד by accident while treating him. The first opinion says the עבד still goes free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The master did not mean to harm. He was trying to help. Even so, the תנא קמא says the עבד goes free, because the master's action caused the injury.

keyTerms.meaning: To put medicine or paint on the eye
He laughed at the master (the master's help backfired)

phrases.aramaic: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה רַבּוֹ רוֹפֵא,
phrases.english: The Sages taught: If his master was a doctor,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לוֹ לִכְחוֹל לוֹ עֵינוֹ וְסִמְּאָהּ,
phrases.english: and he told him to put medicine on his eye, and he blinded it,
phrases.notes: The slave is the one asking, and the master is the one who blinds.

phrases.english: [or] to drill his tooth, and he knocked it out —
he has laughed at the master, and he goes out to freedom.
phrases.notes: The master meant to help, but the slave ends up the winner and walks away free.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיָה רַבּוֹ רוֹפֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about whether the master must intend the harm.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, an עבד hurt by his master during medical treatment goes free, even though the master did not mean to hurt him.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: the master must intend to destroy
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל disagrees. He reads the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ in the פסוק as meaning the עבד goes free only if the master intended to destroy the eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: The פסוק says 'and destroys it,' which means he does not go free unless the master intended to destroy it.
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion in the same ברייתא disagrees with the first. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says an accident during treatment does not free the עבד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He learns from the פסוק's word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ that the master must mean to destroy. A doctor trying to heal had no such intent, so the עבד stays an עבד.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with the first opinion here
And destroys it (a word from the פסוק)

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
"And destroys it" — [he goes free] only if he intends to destroy it.
phrases.notes: שמות 21:26

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing opinion within the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עבד goes free only if the master intended to destroy the eye or tooth.

steps.title: What do the Sages learn from 'and destroys it'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the רבנן do not require intent, so what do they learn from the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Rabbis, what do they do with this word 'and destroys it'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question to set up the next step. If the רבנן don't learn 'intent' from this word, what is it there for?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל used וְשִׁחֲתָהּ to require intent. The רבנן disagree, but every word in the פסוק must teach something. So the גמרא wants to know what the רבנן learn from it.

keyTerms.meaning: And the Sages (here, the first opinion in the ברייתא)
What do they do with it? (What do they learn from it?)

phrases.english: And the Rabbis, this [word] "and destroys it",
what do they do with it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the רבנן explain the word that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל relied on.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the רבנן learn from the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ, since they don't use it to require intent.

steps.title: The Sages use it for the unborn baby case
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן use וְשִׁחֲתָהּ for רבי אלעזר's case. A master who reaches into his pregnant שפחה and blinds the unborn baby is exempt, because he never meant to harm the baby's eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: They need it for what was taught: רבי אלעזר says, if a master put his hand into the womb of his maidservant and blinded the baby inside her, he is exempt. What is the reason? Because the verse says 'and destroys it,' meaning only if he intends to destroy it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. The רבנן do learn something from וְשִׁחֲתָהּ, just for a different case: blinding an unborn baby.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the doctor case, the master was working on the eye itself, so the רבנן say the עבד goes free. In רבי אלעזר's case, the master was helping with the birth and was not aiming at the baby's eye at all. So the רבנן use וְשִׁחֲתָהּ to exclude only this kind of case.

keyTerms.meaning: They need it (for a different teaching)

steps.confusionAlert: Both sides use the same word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ. The difference is how far it reaches. For רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, it excludes even a doctor working on the eye. For the רבנן, it excludes only a case like the baby, where the master wasn't aiming at the eye at all.
steps.whatToRemember: The תנא קמא frees an עבד even when a doctor master hurt him by accident. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל requires intent to destroy. The רבנן use וְשִׁחֲתָהּ only for the unborn baby case.

phrases.english: They need it for that which was taught [in a ברייתא]:
Rabbi Elazar says:
If he put his hand into the womb of his maidservant
and blinded the baby inside her, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: He means the baby does not go free when it is born.

phrases.english: What is the reason? Because the verse says:
"And destroys it" — only if he intends to destroy it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיבְּעֵי לְהוּ לְכִדְתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן use וְשִׁחֲתָהּ to exempt a master who blinded an unborn baby while reaching into the womb, since he never aimed at its eye.

steps.title: How does רבן שמעון בן גמליאל learn רבי אלעזר's case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל gets רבי אלעזר's case, since he already used the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ to require intent.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? (Where does רבן שמעון בן גמליאל learn the case of the unborn baby?)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and asks where he learns רבי אלעזר's case. This one-word question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 25 the רבנן used וְשִׁחֲתָהּ for the unborn baby. But רבן שמעון בן גמליאל already used that same word to require intent, so the word seems to be used up for him. The גמרא wants to know his source for רבי אלעזר's case.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one? A short way of asking how the other opinion handles this point

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: This means רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: how does he learn the unborn baby case, if he already used וְשִׁחֲתָהּ for intent?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After seeing the רבנן's use of וְשִׁחֲתָהּ, the גמרא asks how רבן שמעון בן גמליאל learns the same case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source רבן שמעון בן גמליאל uses for רבי אלעזר's case of blinding the unborn baby.

steps.title: He learns it from the extra ending of the word
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל learns רבי אלעזר's case from the fact that the פסוק says שִׁחֲתָהּ, 'destroys it,' and not just שִׁחֵת, 'destroys.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns it from the difference between 'and destroys' (וְשִׁחֵת) and 'destroys it' (שִׁחֲתָהּ).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל gets a second lesson from the same word. The extra 'it' at the end of the word teaches רבי אלעזר's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק could have said just וְשִׁחֵת, 'and destroys.' Instead it says וְשִׁחֲתָהּ, 'and destroys it.' רבן שמעון בן גמליאל uses the basic word for intent and the extra 'it' for the unborn baby, so he gets both lessons.

keyTerms.meaning: It comes out from / it is learned from

phrases.english: He learns it from 'and destroys' versus 'destroys it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל learns רבי אלעזר's case from the extra ending of שִׁחֲתָהּ compared with plain שִׁחֵת.

steps.title: Why don't the רבנן use that same extra ending?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the רבנן do not accept the reading of שִׁחֵת and שִׁחֲתָהּ.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? (Why don't the רבנן learn anything from 'destroys' versus 'destroys it'?)
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא turns to the רבנן and asks about this extra ending. This sets up the final answer of the back-and-forth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the extra ending can teach something, the רבנן could use it for רבי אלעזר's case. Then the main word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ would be free to teach intent, as רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says. The גמרא asks why the רבנן do not do this.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one? Here it turns back to the רבנן

phrases.english: And the other one?
phrases.notes: Now this means the רבנן: why don't they learn anything from the extra ending?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the question from step 26 around and asks it about the רבנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the רבנן do not learn anything from the difference between שִׁחֵת and שִׁחֲתָהּ.

steps.title: The רבנן do not read meaning into that difference
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן do not learn anything from the difference between שִׁחֵת and שִׁחֲתָהּ. To them it is not a real change in wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: They do not learn anything from 'destroys' versus 'destroys it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the רבנן simply do not learn anything from the extra ending. This closes the discussion about the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two sides disagree about how to read the פסוק. For the רבנן, the extra ending is just normal wording, so the word וְשִׁחֲתָהּ teaches only one thing, the unborn baby case. That leaves them no source for requiring intent, so a doctor who blinds his עבד by accident still frees him.

keyTerms.meaning: He does not learn anything from it; he does not treat it as a source

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree to רבי אלעזר's case of the unborn baby. They disagree about the extra ending of שִׁחֲתָהּ. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל learns from it, so he can also require intent. The רבנן do not, so they do not require intent.

phrases.english: He does not learn anything from 'destroys' versus 'destroys it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28 and ends the discussion between the רבנן and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The רבנן do not learn anything from the difference between שִׁחֵת and שִׁחֲתָהּ.

steps.title: Removing an eye that was already blind frees the עבד
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rules that if a master removes an עבד's eye that was already blind, the עבד goes free. The reason is that he is now missing a limb.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: If an עבד's eye was blind and his master removed it, the עבד goes free because of it. Why? Because now he is missing a limb.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ruling from רב ששת. A blind eye still counts, and if the master removes it, the עבד goes free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think a blind eye is already worthless, so removing it takes nothing away. רב ששת says that being missing a whole limb is worse than having a limb that does not work. So taking out the blind eye is a real new injury.

keyTerms.meaning: He dug it out / removed it

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think a blind eye 'doesn't count.' Even though it could not see, removing it leaves the עבד missing a limb, and that is enough to set him free.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
If his eye was blind, and the master removed it –
the slave goes out to freedom through them.
What is the reason? He is missing a limb.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion about וְשִׁחֲתָהּ has ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Removing an already-blind eye frees the עבד, because he is now missing a limb.

steps.title: A ברייתא: birds are not disqualified by blemishes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support רב ששת. It says that animal קרבנות must be without a blemish and male, but bird קרבנות do not need either.
steps.simpleTranslation: And a ברייתא also taught: being without a blemish and being male are required for animals, but not for birds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins bringing support for רב ששת from a ברייתא about קרבנות. This first part sets up the rule, and the proof itself comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא starts with the general rule: a bird קרבן does not need to be free of blemishes. This sets up the question of whether anything at all disqualifies a bird. The answer will show that missing a limb is in a different, more serious category than a regular blemish.

keyTerms.meaning: And a תנא also taught this (a ברייתא supports the point)

phrases.english: And a tanna taught it too:
Being unblemished and being male apply to animals,
phrases.notes: This is about קרבנות: an animal offering must be without a blemish, and some offerings must be male.

phrases.english: but being unblemished and being male do not apply to birds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts bringing a ברייתא to support רב ששת's ruling.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's rule that missing a limb is worse than a blemish.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about which animals and birds may be brought as קרבנות.

steps.title: A bird missing a limb, such as a removed eye, is disqualified
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא teaches from the words 'from the birds' that a bird with a dried-up wing, a cut-off leg or a removed eye is not acceptable. This shows that a missing eye is more serious than a regular blemish, which supports רב ששת.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think a bird is still fine if its wing dried up, its leg was cut off, or its eye was removed. So the פסוק says 'from the birds,' meaning not every bird.
steps.whatsHappening: This finishes the proof for רב ששת. Even though blemishes do not disqualify birds, a bird with a removed eye is disqualified.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Birds are not disqualified by ordinary blemishes, but they are disqualified when a limb is missing. A removed eye is on that list, so a missing eye is more serious than a regular blemish. In the same way, removing a blind eye takes away a whole limb, so the עבד goes free.
steps.whatToRemember: Missing a limb is more serious than having a blemish. A bird with a removed eye is disqualified even though ordinary blemishes do not disqualify birds. So removing an עבד's blind eye counts as a real injury and sets him free.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the law sees a missing limb as its own serious category, apart from a limb that does not work. That is the key idea behind רב ששת's ruling.

phrases.english: You might think that if its wing dried up,
its leg was cut off, or its eye was removed, it is still fine?
So the verse says: 'from the birds' –
phrases.notes: ויקרא 1:14

phrases.english: and not every bird.
phrases.notes: 'From' means only some birds, so a bird missing a limb is left out.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא started in step 31 and gives the actual proof for רב ששת.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's rule that removing a blind eye frees the עבד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא learns from 'מִן הָעוֹף' that a bird missing a limb, including a removed eye, is disqualified, even though ordinary blemishes do not disqualify birds.

steps.title: רב begins a new ruling about the slave
steps.stepSummary: רב חייא בר אשי quotes רב, who starts to describe a case where the עבד 'had' something. The case itself continues in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חייא בר אשי says in the name of רב: If the slave had...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is opening a new statement from רב, passed on by רב חייא בר אשי. This line only sets up the case, and the ruling comes right after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the גמרא has dealt with injuries that free an עבד, and it just backed up רב ששת about a blind eye. Now רב begins describing something the עבד 'had', which tells us a new case is about to be presented. We have to wait for the next words to learn what he had and what the law is.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who often passes on teachings of רב
The great early אמורא in Babylonia, whose ruling is being quoted
'He had', the opening words of the case being described

steps.confusionAlert: Do not try to work out the ruling from these words alone. The sentence is cut off here and only finishes in the next part of the גמרא.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi says that Rav says:
If the slave had

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִיָּיא בַּר אָשֵׁי אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the support for רב ששת's ruling about a blind eye, the גמרא opens a new statement from רב about another injury case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ruling is not yet stated. This line only opens the case of something the עבד 'had', and the rest continues in the next part.
